title: Meet the Italian Shoe Designer Who Collects Art by Andy Warhol, Barbara Kruger, and More
summary: Walk into a church in Naples, Italy, and you might stumble across a Caravaggio or an Artemisia Gentileschi . For Italian shoe designer and collector Ernesto Esposito, that proximity to beauty shaped everything that followed. “I grew up in Naples, a city where beauty is not confined to museums but is part of everyday life,” Esposito said. “Art came first. Long before becoming a shoe designer, I was already fascinated by beauty, proportions, and the emotional power of objects.” Esposito began his career in the 1970s with renowned shoemaker Sergio Rossi. His own collections pair classic silhouettes with more daring designs, including towering open-toe heels in leopard-print pony hair and red patent leather. Over several decades, he has also built an art collection featuring works by Katharina Grosse , Richard Prince , John Baldessari , Andy Warhol , Joseph Beuys , Cindy Sherman , Barbara Kruger , and George Condo , alongside those by younger painters such as Leonardo Devito and Adam Handler . For Esposito, collecting is not simply about ownership, taste, or market value. It is a way of living with questions, memories, friendships, and creative risk. Starting with Warhol His first acquisition was a limited-edition silkscreen from Warhol’s 1971 “ Electric Chair ” series. “I did not choose it because it was fashionable, nor as an investment,” he said. “I bought it because it moved me deeply. It is a work that is at once beautiful, unsettling, and profoundly human.” That instinct has guided him ever since. “Great art does not provide answers, but instead asks questions that continue to stay with you throughout your life,” he said. “That work defined the direction of my entire collection.” Growing up amid Naples’s layered history taught Esposito that objects could carry meaning beyond their function. “When I became a designer, I never considered a shoe to be merely a product,” he said. “To me, a shoe is a cultural object, capable of expressing identity, emotion, and creativity.” He sees a direct connection between art and fashion. “All of my work in fashion has always been guided by the same curiosity and sensitivity that first made me fall in love with art,” he said. Esposito also resists a simple distinction between craftsman and artist. “Great craftsmen possess artistic sensitivity, while great artists often have extraordinary mastery of technique,” he said. “Excellence is always born from the meeting of imagination and skill.” Building an art collection of sensibilities What unifies his collection is not a theme or medium, but a sensibility. “I am drawn to artists who possess an authentic and recognizable language,” he said. “I do not collect a particular style, but rather personalities.” His approach was shaped in part by the legendary Neapolitan dealer and curator Lucio Amelio. “Meeting Lucio opened an entirely new world to me,” Esposito said. “Through him, I met extraordinary artists and discovered that art does not simply serve to decorate a space, but can change the way we look at and understand reality.” Collecting, he said, then became “an integral part of the way I live and interpret the world.” For Esposito, buying art requires conviction. “A true collector is someone who takes responsibility,” he said. “They choose according to their own instinct, not according to market consensus.” One artist currently holding his attention is De Vito. Esposito admires “the consistency of his research, the quality of his painterly language, and his ability to address contemporary themes without chasing trends.” Following a young artist’s development, he added, “is one of the most fascinating aspects of collecting.” Collecting emerging and established artists alongside each other Little Runner Abduction, 2026 Adam Handler Trium Art Gallery He refuses to rank emerging talent against established masters. “The great masters represent the memory and history of art, while emerging artists bring energy, freedom, and unpredictability,” he said. In a market saturated with spectacle, sincerity still moves him most. “The works that truly stay with us are those still capable of conveying a personal truth,” he said. “Authenticity remains the rarest quality.” Art’s influence on his footwear is rarely literal. “Sometimes it is a color combination, other times a proportion, or perhaps the courage to make an unexpected decision,” he said. “The influence of art is constant, often unconscious, but always present.” Designing and collecting may appear to arise from the same impulse, but Esposito experiences them differently. “Designing allows me to create. Collecting allows me to listen,” he said. “When I design, I am the one making decisions. When I collect, I enter into dialogue with someone else’s vision.” His most recent direct collaboration was a residency with American painter Adam Handler. Handler reminded him of a young Keith Haring , whom Esposito met in New York early in Haring’s career. “It is not a stylistic comparison,” Esposito said, “but rather the energy, enthusiasm, and total dedication to work that I recognized again in Adam.” Staged with Trium Art Gallery in Monza, Italy, and Noh-Art , the residency became more than a commission. Esposito credited Naples—its light, history, energy, and openness—with transforming it into “something far deeper than a simple artistic collaboration.” “The work itself is certainly important, but what truly remains is the experience shared together,” he said. “Artists need places capable of inspiring them, authentic encounters, and human relationships.” Looking ahead, Esposito imagines future residencies with artists chosen not for their market standing, but for their openness: “an artist capable of being surprised by Naples just as much as Naples could be surprised by them.” It is from that encounter, he believes, that “the most authentic projects can emerge.”

title: Artist Betye Saar dies at 99.
summary: Artist Betye Saar , whose assemblages transformed ephemera and heirlooms into meditations on Black history, racism, memory, and spirituality, died in her sleep on July 26 in Los Angeles, four days before her 100th birthday. Her death was confirmed by Roberts Projects , the Los Angeles gallery that represented her for close to two decades. “Betye Saar was one of the greatest artists of our time, and it has been an immense honor to work with her for nearly 20 years,” Julie Roberts, co-founder of Roberts Projects, said in a statement. “Her singular vision transformed the course of contemporary art, and her legacy will continue to inspire generations of artists, scholars, and audiences around the world.” Born Betye Irene Brown in Los Angeles in 1926, Saar was the eldest of three children of Jefferson Maze Brown and Beatrice Lillian Parson. Her father died when she was about five, and her mother moved the family to Pasadena to live with a maternal aunt, Hattie Parson Keys, whose belongings later inspired a series of assemblages made in her honor. Saar spent summers at her paternal grandparents’ home in the Watts neighborhood in L.A., watching artist Simon Rodia construct his monumental architectural sculpture Watts Towers by hand, inspiring Saar’s passion for using found and repurposed materials. Saar studied design at UCLA and worked for years as an interior decorator, at one point running a studio called Brown and Tann with fellow designer Curtis Tann. In 1952, she married ceramicist Richard Saar; the couple settled in Laurel Canyon, Hollywood Hills, and had three daughters, Lezley, Alison , and Tracye, before divorcing in the late 1960s. Saar remained in the Laurel Canyon house for the rest of her life. The Long Memory, 1998 Betye Saar CLAMP Her turn toward fine art came almost by chance. Enrolled at Cal State Long Beach to pursue a teaching credential, Saar wandered into the printmaking studio and immediately changed course. “The move into fine art, it was liberating,” she later told the Los Angeles Times . “It gave me freedom to experiment.” Her early prints carried mystical and occult overtones, drawn from books on alchemy and palmistry, and she began framing them in old window frames scavenged from junk shops. A 1967 exhibition of Joseph Cornell ’s boxed assemblages at the Pasadena Art Museum pushed Saar toward three dimensions. In 1969, she completed Black Girl’s Window , built around a salvaged window frame layering autobiographical imagery, astrology, and racial identity. Trips to Chicago’s Field Museum, where she immersed herself in African art, and to Haiti in the early 1970s, where she explored voodoo and folk magic, further shaped her visual language. Saar’s best-known work, The Liberation of Aunt Jemima (1972), transformed a stereotypical “mammy” figurine—armed with a rifle and grenade—into what she described as a warrior against servitude. First shown at the Rainbow Sign, a Black cultural center in Berkeley, California, near the headquarters of the Black Panthers, the piece connected Saar to the Black Arts Movement and led to a solo exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1975. Activist Angela Davis later credited it with helping to spur the Black women’s movement. “I wanted to empower her,” Saar said in a 2015 interview . “I wanted to make her a warrior.” The original assemblage now belongs to the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive . 4 Doors in a Window (Bellagio, Italy - 1994), 2004 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Over the following decades, Saar continued mining flea markets, yard sales, and family heirlooms, producing works including Records for Hattie (1975), Mojotech (1987), and the altarpiece Wings of Morning (1992), alongside installations like House of Fortune (1988). Scholar Kellie Jones, who curated the 2011 exhibition “Now Dig This! Art and Black Los Angeles 1960–1980” at the Hammer Museum , said in a TK that Saar’s reach extended well beyond the U.S.: “She has works with Mexican milagros, she has titles in Spanish, she at certain points has Asian influence and Haitian influence... She was a person in the world.” Her practice inspired a generation of artists, including her daughter, the artist Alison Saar. Saar’s work is held in the collections of more than 80 institutions worldwide, and she had solo exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Fondazione Prada in Milan, as well as the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and the California African American Museum. “I’ve always done what I did and never felt I was competing with what was going on,” she told the Los Angeles Times of her career. She continued working into her late 90s, including a commissioned installation at the Huntington Library’s gardens, made at 96 and now on view as “Betye Saar: Drifting Toward Twilight” through November 2027. “Even in death those things can be really beautiful,” she said of the installation in an accompanying documentary. Two other shows remain on view during her centennial year: “ Let’s Get It On: The Wearable Art of Betye Saar ” at Roberts Projects, in Los Angeles, through August 22, and “Betye Saar’s Black Dolls” at the New York Historical Society, through October 4. Her works are currently included in “ Tarot! Renaissance Symbols, Modern Visions ” at the Morgan Library & Museum. Saar is survived by her daughters, Lezley Saar, Alison Saar, and Tracye Saar-Cavanaugh, as well as six grandchildren, including the artist Maddy Inez , and a pet tortoise named Rojo. Her artistic legacy is now overseen by the Betye Saar Legacy Group , a coalition of scholars and curators the artist assembled in 2025 with Roberts Projects. A biography by Zoé Whitley, co-curator of “Soul of a Nation: Art in the Age of Black Power,” is expected in 2027.

title: Guggenheim Abu Dhabi announces 2026 opening date.
summary: The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi will open to the public on December 11, Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism has announced. First announced in 2006, the museum is one of the most anticipated museum openings in decades. Designed by the late Frank Gehry , the building is defined by ten sculptural cones rising to heights of up to 88 metres. Nine are surrounded by stainless steel mesh, providing natural ventilation and shade while giving the structure its distinctive skyline. Its 30 galleries, across 11,600 square meters of interior space, are connected by a central atrium, with a further 23,000 square meters of outdoor exhibition areas. The total built-up area totals 80,000 square metres, the largest of the four Guggenheim locations. The museum will focus on modern and contemporary art from the 1960s to the present, with a particular emphasis on North Africa, and West and South Asia. Rather than presenting art chronologically, the collection will be organised around thematic and geographic groupings. Among the sections are “Abstractions,” “Popular Culture,” “Land,” and “Language and Storytelling.” The collection has been in development since 2009. Guggenheim Abu Dhabi joins the Guggenheim Foundation’s constellation of museums in New York , Venice , and Bilbao , while maintaining, its organisers say, a distinct identity rooted in the cultural and historical position of the United Arab Emirates. It is located on Saadiyat Island, where several high profile museums have opened in recent years, such as Louvre Abu Dhabi, the Zayed National Museum, Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi . “The Guggenheim Foundation is proud and delighted to be a longstanding partner with the Department of Culture and Tourism –Abu Dhabi in shaping a museum of contemporary art of magnificent scope and aspiration,” said Dr. Mariët Westermann, director and CEO of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, in a statement. “The museum’s art collection is uniquely local and global, centered in the region but with works from all continents.”

title: National Portrait Gallery acquires Harley Weir’s portrait of Charli XCX.
summary: The National Portrait Gallery in London has acquired a portrait of pop star Charli XCX by British photographer Harley Weir . The photograph, which was shot in 2024, will be added to the museum’s collection this week. The untitled work shows the singer leaning against a wall in a white crop top and unbuttoned black jeans and is now on view in the gallery’s History Makers Now space, which spotlights figures who have shaped contemporary culture. The image became one of the defining pictures of Charli’s Brat era, the 2024 album that turned her into a mainstream phenomenon on the strength of its candor and “debauched swagger,” as the BBC described it . The acquisition was funded by a gift from the Bukhman Foundation. “Harley Weir has developed a distinctive photographic language that combines intimacy with a powerful sense of presence,” said Brandei Estes, the gallery’s senior curator of photographs. “We are delighted to acquire this striking portrait of Charli XCX, which captures one of the defining cultural figures of her generation.” The acquisition arrives the same week Charli released her eighth album, Music, Fashion, Film , built around chopped-up guitar samples and distorted melodies that find her reflecting on fame and artistic identity in Brat ’s aftermath. Portraits of pop stars have been grabbing headlines recently. In March, the National Portrait Gallery acquired West End Girl (Lily Allen) (2025), a painting by Spanish artist Nieves González that doubled as the cover art for Allen’s album of the same name. Charli herself was previously the subject of a portrait by painter Issy Wood , commissioned for the November 2025 cover of Vanity Fair . Beyond music, Charli has been expanding into film, with recent roles in the Polish drama Erupcja , the ensemble film Sacrifice alongside Anya Taylor-Joy and Chris Evans, and the mockumentary The Moment , based on the release of the Brat album. She is set to headline the Reading and Leeds festivals in the U.K. next month before a North American tour in the fall.

title: Georgia O’Keeffe Ghost Ranch paintings to go on display in the U.K. for the first time in 2027.
summary: The Courtauld Gallery in London will open “ Georgia O’Keeffe : Ghost Ranch” in October 2027, an exhibition of nearly two dozen works that explore how the American artist’s New Mexico property shaped her painting practice. Most of the works have never been exhibited in the U.K., according to the Guardian , which first reported the news. Only six of the roughly two dozen paintings in the exhibition have been previously exhibited in Britain, it revealed. Ghost Ranch, a remote property in the high desert north of Santa Fe, became O’Keeffe’s summer home starting in 1934, when she began renting a room on the 21,000-acre estate before eventually purchasing it. “As soon as I saw it, that was my country,” she once said. “I’d never seen anything like it before, but it fitted to me exactly.” Dr. Karen Serres, senior curator of paintings at the Courtauld, told the Guardian that O’Keeffe’s relationship to Ghost Ranch remains under-recognized in Britain despite its centrality to her work. “Ghost Ranch was such an important part of her life, and it illuminates a large part of her art in general,” Serres said, pointing to works like Red and Yellow Cliffs (1940) and Gerald’s Tree I (1937) as direct responses to the surrounding landscape. The show also arrives against a history of uneven critical reception to O’Keeffe in the U.K. In 1993, a Hayward Gallery exhibition drew dismissive reviews from British critics, and more recently, the reception to her 2016 Tate Modern show was largely framed around disputing assumptions that her flower paintings depicted female genitalia. “She’s known as just this formidable female artist,” said Serres. “But actually seeing her work, understanding what she’s about, I don’t think we are there yet.” The Courtauld exhibition follows a fresh wave of attention to O’Keeffe elsewhere. The Detroit Institute of Arts opens “Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture” on September 11th, an exhibition of nearly 40 works examining her engagement with the built environment, from Manhattan skyscrapers to New Mexico adobe structures, anchored by Stables (1932), which is owned by the museum. On October 3rd, Hauser & Wirth inaugurates its new Palo Alto gallery with “Calder | O’Keeffe,” the first exhibition devoted to the artist’s decades-long friendship with Alexander Calder , developed with the Calder Foundation and the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. A documentary about the artist , directed by Academy Award– and Emmy Award–winning filmmakers Paul Wagner and Ellen Casey Wagner, was also released earlier this year.

title: Legendary Gallerist Claes Nordenhake on Artists, Arguments, and 50 Years in the Art Business
summary: “As a young gallerist, I was a cleaner, a security guard, an interiordesigner, a carpenter, a courier, a warehouse manager, and a stock clerk,” said Claes Nordenhake, the Swedish art dealer whose eponymous enterprise, Galerie Nordenhake , celebrates its half-century this year. Over five decades, the business has grown from a modest space opened in 1976 in Malmö on the southern coast of Sweden, showing contemporary art—favoring Minimalist , often conceptual, works—into a powerhouse brand with galleries in Stockholm, Berlin, and Mexico City. Talking to Artsy from his Berlin branch, Nordenhake’s stocktake of his early duties doesn’t end there. Starting out, he was obliged to be a photographer, philosopher, business strategist, psychotherapist, and a divorce counselor, he explained. He could be a “sympathetic drinking buddy” one day and an “arrogant bastard” the next. And, when the occasion allowed, he was an art dealer. Roots in Malmö Nordenhake was born in 1948 and grew up in the Skåne region of southern Sweden, where his family owned several quarries celebrated for their Ebony Black granite—a material highly sought after by artists such as Isamu Noguchi and Max Bill . “Coming from a rather conventional business family, sort of a bourgeois upbringing, the artists that I encountered offered another different view on life,” he noted. And there was art at home. “My old man had a collection of mainly Swedish artists, but at some point, he got absolutely fascinated by Lucio Fontana . He had three paintings: one red, one white, and one blue. Fontana in the 1960s was like the ultimate avant-garde.” Green Felt Piece, 1983-84 Robert Morris Galerie Nordenhake Wandrelief, 1988 Ulrich Rückriem Galerie Nordenhake Nordenhake initially trained as a lawyer but quit his studies to pursue his interest in art. I suggest that Malmö in the 1970s could hardly have been a center of Conceptual art . “No, for sure. But the advantage of Malmö was that it was very close to the rest of Europe,” Nordenhake explained. “I would drive my car, and if I left Malmö in the morning, I would be in Cologne in the afternoon or evening. It would take the same time from Malmö to Stockholm.” He targeted a “cosmopolitan” clientele. “There were maybe five collectors who were interested in international art and wanted to be part of that scene,” he said. “I was convinced of certain things. I was very interested in Concrete art …and I made these few collectors follow my interest.” He kept costs low—“hand to mouth”—and acquired a reputation for showing monochrome paintings by internationally renowned artists such as Robert Mangold , Alan Uglow , and Marcia Hafif , as well as Minimalist sculptures by Robert Morris and Ulrich Rückriem . Closer to home, he championed the work of the Swedish modernist painter Olle Bærtling . “He was absolutely exceptional,” recalled Nordenhake. “He was working with colors that, I mean…the blue would never be the blue of the sky, the green never the green of the grass. They were sorts of fields of energy.” How Nordenhake expanded its footprint The business moved to Stockholm in the mid-1980s, when Nordenhake was offered a “sensational space” in the Royal Academy of Fine Arts building. “I’m sure there were a lot of discussions in the gallery about whether one should let the enemy into the house?” he said, laughing, referring to the inclusion—or contamination—of a commercial gallery in a museum context. The rooms allowed him to present larger sculptures, including works by Richard Serra . In 2000 he opened in Berlin, when the city had become a magnet for both artists and gallerists taking advantage of the low rents for studios and a sense of zeitgeist. “I thought it would have been easier,” he recalled. “It was an experiment to come with three kids and my wife and move the entire family. I come from a shit-kicking little town in southern Sweden, so I have no experience of big cities.” At the time, Berlin’s reputation as an artistic hotbed following the fall of the Wall was more than a cliché, said Nordenhake, at least to begin with. “From 1990 to 2010, even a young artist could find an apartment and a studio rather easily,” Nordenhake said. Collectors would visit from abroad to experience the scene. Rents rose over the subsequent years, and the tone shifted. But Nordenhake has helped to foster a collegiate atmosphere among the city’s galleries. In 2005, he co-founded (with Max Hetzler) the first Gallery Weekend Berlin , which, two decades later, now includes some 50 participating galleries and has become a template copied in major cities around the world. Nordenhake opened a third gallery in 2018 in Mexico City, on the suggestion of his former intern, Toni Sadurní Viñas (the gallery’s current director). “Mexico City is the new Berlin,” he declared. “ At the beginning of this century and until recently, Berlin was a place where artists, even young artists, could afford both a studio and an apartment. Which is still the case in Mexico City.” And, he noted, the general public appreciates its artistic heritage, “from the pre-Columbian artifacts to Frida Kahlo and the muralists. Art means something for Mexicans.” Lessons from 50 years in the art trade Is it easy to work with artists over a long period? “I would say usually no. But of course, there are always exceptions,” he smiled. The artist-gallerist relationship is similar to a “marriage,” he said, with all the “conflicts” that implies. And being a gallerist is a work in progress. “You learn stuff,” he noted, adding that his opinion on artists’ work can change over time. “I’m much more generous than I used to be. My art world has gotten bigger.” “Contemporary art is a notoriously slippery commodity in which to do business,” said Philip Hook, author of Rogues’ Gallery, a History of Art and its Dealers . “Very few art dealers remain at the forefront of the avant-garde beyond one generation.” Claes’s son, Sten, is now a director at Galerie Nordenhake, offering a future path for a gallery that needs exceptional mental and commercial agility to continue interpreting the ever-changing new. This is illustrated by the gallery’s 50th anniversary group exhibitions, staged across its three locations, showing artists from its past and present roster, from Bærtling’s last known painting, Ksard (1980), to newly commissioned works by Lap-See Lam (winner of the prestigious Lise Wilhelmsen Art Award last year). And while he is aware of the challenges—both commercially and intellectually—Nordenhake stated that “curiosity is the most amazing driving force. I’m a traveling salesman and a schoolteacher.” Just two more professions to add to his list.

title: 7 Unforgettable Art Day Trips Worth Taking in Summer 2026
summary: Summer 2026 is in full swing, and it’s been an exciting one so far, with highlights ranging from the FIFA World Cup to The Odyssey . But as we enter the quieter phase of the season, your calendar might be a little more open, making it the perfect time to add an art excursion to your summer agenda. Though some art acolytes will certainly be venturing to visit the Venice Biennale 2026 , by and large, the summer is a sleepier season for the art world’s major cities. It’s thus a good time of year to get off the beaten path and take a detour. Day trips, by car, train, or ferry, are an easy way to experience art at a slower, more focused pace. We’ve put together a list of seven standout institutions reachable from major cities—all accessible with little effort. At each of these destinations, you’ll find idyllic settings, world-class architecture, and unforgettable art. This summer, there are can’t-miss exhibitions on view, too, from Issy Wood ’s first Nordic museum show at the Kistefos Museum in Norway to Anicka Yi ’s first large-scale outdoor project at Storm King in upstate New York. Instituto Inhotim Brumadinho, Minas Gerais, Brazil Getting there: About an hour away by car from Belo Horizonte, Brazil, served by Confins International Airport. Wander the sprawling open-air museum and gardens of Brazil’s Instituto Inhotim as birds fly overhead and tropical plants provide a canopy of green. Founded in 2004 by collector Bernardo Paz and set in the verdant hills of Minas Gerais, Instituto Inhotim opened to the public in 2006. There is no place else quite like it. Occupying over 5,000 acres, the institute is both a nature preserve, home to over 1,000 plant species, and a singular art venue encompassing sculpture gardens and close to two dozen galleries showing both permanent collection and temporary exhibitions. Currently, over 900 works by 50 artists are on view. Inhotim turns 20 in 2026, and it’s marking the anniversary with new site-specific commissions as well as with the return of The Murder of Crows (2008), Janet Cardiff and George Bures Miller ’s 98-speaker sound installation later this fall. These will be on view alongside works by Cildo Meireles , Doris Salcedo , Matthew Barney , and Hélio Oiticica , among others. Storm King Art Center New Windsor, New York Getting there: About 90 minutes from New York City by car, or by Metro-North train plus a shuttle. Less than two hours from the hubbub of midtown Manhattan lies Storm King, a 500-acre sculpture park situated on rolling meadows. Here, one can easily spend a day wandering on foot, discovering monumental sculptures and installations around every corner. Among the perennial highlights are Maya Lin ’s rolling hill Storm King Wavefield (2009), Alexander Calder ’s towering red steel Five Swords (1976) , and Menashe Kadishman ’s Suspended (1977), which is among the center’s most popular photo ops. Opened to the public in 1960, the pioneering outdoor space continues to embrace contemporary art with yearly temporary exhibitions. The 2026 season brings Anicka Yi’s first large-scale outdoor project, an installation of towering acrylic columns filled with organic matter set into a seven-acre field. Also on view are artist Saif Azzuz ’s steel-and-salvage sturgeon and artist Liz Glynn ’s concrete casts of Gilded Age furniture. For ambitious art lovers, the trip can be paired with a visit to Dia Beacon, 20 minutes away across the river, for a combination of outdoor and indoor Minimalist and land art in a single trip. The 2026 season runs through November 9th. Kistefos Museum Jevnaker, Norway Getting there: About an hour’s drive or express bus from Oslo. As visitors approach, the Kistefos Museum’s building is likely to stop visitors dead in their tracks. Set along the Randselva river, the stunning museum, designed by the Bjarke Ingels Group, is known as “The Twist.” The massive building, glass at one end, folded aluminum on the other, represents just that, twisting its horizontal form across the length of the river. At once a gallery, a sculpture, and a bridge, the structure is an architectural destination in its own right. But that’s just the start. The museum is home to a sculpture park built around a 19th-century wood-pulp mill (old machinery is still visible, as is timber and turbines). Currently, more than 50 outdoor works are located along the riverbank and surrounding forest; these include a new 13-ton bronze by Dana Schutz , her largest work to date. A new Marguerite Humeau commission will be arriving this fall. This year, museum exhibitions are also noteworthy. Issy Wood ’s first major exhibition in the Nordic region, titled “Fish, Fish, Duck,” is currently on view. The show brings together a selection of Wood’s seductive and restrained compositions that draw from the internet, advertising, auction catalogues, and popular culture to create uneasy images that tap into questions of desire and power. Noah Purifoy Outdoor Desert Art Museum Joshua Tree, California Getting there: About two hours from Los Angeles by car. The site is unstaffed, so visit during daylight and bring water. For those who want an unmediated art experience in the American desert, the Noah Purifoy Outdoor Desert Art Museum is an ideal destination. At an unmarked turnoff on a dirt road in the Mojave Desert lies a sprawling 10-acre sculpture park with works made of bicycle parts, television sets, toilets, and salvaged wood. The American artist Noah Purifoy moved out there in 1989 and spent the last 15 years of his life building the site alone. Purifoy is considered the father of the West Coast assemblage movement. He was influenced in part by the found debris he began working with after the 1965 Watts riot. After decades in Los Angeles, he created the museum as his final and largest body of work. The sprawling work was nearly bulldozed in 2001 before a foundation of his friends stepped in to preserve it. The site is free to visit. There are no tickets or explanatory texts. It’s an increasingly rare opportunity for a raw encounter with an artist’s unadulterated vision at such a scale. Museum SAN Wonju, South Korea Getting there: Roughly 90 minutes to 2 hours from Seoul by car, bus, or train. A car or taxi is recommended for the final stretch to the museum. Located in the Oak Valley, a resort in Gangwon Province, Museum SAN opened in 2013, a space where art and nature could commune. The museum’s name is an acronym, which stands for “space, art, nature.” Today, the museum is one of Korea’s most significant private museums, welcoming hundreds of thousands of visitors every year. Designed by Pritzker Prize–winning Japanese architect Tadao Ando , the museum is an elegant concrete-and-glass structure that seems to emerge from the terrain. Adding to the serene effect are a reflecting pool, a stone garden, and a flower field planted in concentric rings on the grounds. Ando’s relationship with the museum has continued over a decade, with the architect subsequently contributing the Meditation Hall (2018) and Space of Light (2023). In 2025, he revealed his newest structure, Ground , an arched concrete chamber conceived with British artist Antony Gormley , whose works are on view inside. Remarkably, five James Turrell works— Sky Space , Horizon Room , Ganzfeld , Wedgework , and Space Divisio n —are also on permanent view at the museum. But beyond these Turrell environments , the museum has a prominent collection, with a distinct focus on paper artworks ranging from hanji crafts to paper books and everything in between. Glenstone Museum Potomac, Maryland Getting there: Glenstone is about an hour from Washington, D.C., or Baltimore. Admission is free, but timed tickets must be booked online in advance. Glenstone is only 15 miles from downtown Washington, D.C., but it feels a world away. Situated on rolling hills, the museum is a tranquil and contemplative space founded to be a space where art, architecture, and landscape are considered a single work. This year, Glenstone celebrates its 20th year with a host of programming and talks focused on everything from Jeff Koons ’s Split-Rocker (2000) (perhaps the museum’s most iconic work) to the architecture of Charles Gwathmey , who designed Glenstone’s original museum buildings (later expansions by Thomas Phifer and Partners are also marvelous). Also on view are special exhibitions including “ Andrea Bowers, ” an exhibition that brings together over 40 works by the American artist, making it one of the largest exhibitions of Bowers’ work to date. Muzeum Susch Susch, Switzerland Getting there: Susch is just over two hours from Zürich by car or train. In a fairytale-like village of the Swiss Alps lies Muzeum Susch, a museum housed in what once was a medieval monastery and 19th-century brewery. The museum, which opened in 2018, is the project of Polish art collector and philanthropist Grażyna Kulczyk and offers a one-of-a-kind art-viewing experience. The museum is primarily focused women artists, and artworks that focus on matrilineal histories and overlooked histories. Muzeum Susch has more than a dozen permanent installations on view, many site-specific, by artists including Tracey Emin , Monika Sosnowska , and Magdalena Abakanowicz . On view now is “Unraveling,” the first major retrospective of the mid-20th-century Italian artist and activist Mariuccia Secol, tracing seven decades of a practice that moved from painting into aprons, metal scouring pads, and a wedding dress dismantled by hand, a powerful commentary on domestic labor.

title: The New York Knicks’ NBA championship trophy to be displayed at the American Museum of Natural History.
summary: The NBA's iconic Larry O’Brien Championship Trophy, newly engraved with the New York Knicks' championship win, is getting a museum moment. The championship award is going on view at the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH), as part of the exhibition “ For the Win: Objects of Sports Excellence .” The trophy will be unveiled at the museum on July 27th. “For the Win” will be on view through January 3, 2027. Designed by Tiffany & Co. , the trophy depicts a regulation-size basketball entering a net, cast in sterling silver with gold vermeil and weighing about 30 pounds. It bears the name of every NBA champion since 1947 and takes its name from Larry O’Brien, who served as the league’s commissioner from 1975 to 1984. The trophy’s arrival marks a full-circle moment for “For the Win,” which opened in May. Among its roughly 70 objects—spanning 15 sports and nearly 150 years of athletic history—is a basketball-shaped fob presented to former Knicks head coach Red Holzman after the team’s 1973 championship, its last before this year’s win. “When we opened ‘For the Win,’ Red Holzman’s 1973 Knicks championship fob was the piece that connected this city to its basketball past,” said guest curator Vikki Tobak in a statement. “Now the NBA’s Larry O’Brien Trophy arrives with the Knicks’ names freshly engraved on it, and that circle closes in a way we never could have planned.” AMNH president Sean M. Decatur framed the trophy’s arrival as part of a broader moment. “This championship has given New Yorkers an extraordinary moment to celebrate together,” he said, calling the trophy “a powerful symbol of athletic achievement.” Other highlights in “For the Win” include one of Jesse Owens’s gold medals from the 1936 Berlin Olympics , the NFL’s Vince Lombardi Trophy, and the New York Liberty’s 2024 WNBA championship trophy. Tobak curates the exhibition in partnership with Rich Kleiman, the CEO of the sports entertainment company Boardroom, and with Kate Kiseeva, associate curator in the Museum’s Division of Physical Sciences.

title: MFA Boston to host exclusive U.S. Pierre-Auguste Renoir exhibition in February 2027.
summary: Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette (Bal du moulin de la galette), 1876 Pierre-Auguste Renoir Musée d'Orsay The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston will be the only U.S. venue for “Renoir and Love,” opening February 28, 2027—a once-in-a-generation exhibition co-organized with the Musée d’Orsay in Paris and the National Gallery in London , and billed as the first show devoted specifically to the theme of love in Renoir’s work. It is also the museum’s first major Pierre-Auguste Renoir exhibition in more than four decades. The show will bring together 40 paintings from collections around the world and will be on view through June 13, 2027. “Renoir and Love” centers on the two decades between the mid-1860s and mid-1880s, a period the museum considers the height of Renoir’s output, when the artist turned repeatedly to themes of friendship, family, and flirtation rather than the moralizing or anecdotal subjects favored by some of his Impressionist peers. The exhibition argues that Renoir’s scenes of gardens, cafés, and theaters were among his greatest masterpieces. . Highlights include Dance at Moulin de la Galette (1876), on loan from the Musée d’Orsay, shown alongside its companion painting, Dance in the Country (1883), also from the d’Orsay, and the MFA’s own Dance at Bougival (1883). Also on view are At Renoir’s Home (1876), which depicts the sociability of the artist’s studio, and Madame Monet and Her Son (1874), which points to Renoir’s friendship with fellow Impressionist Claude Monet . The show also arrives amid renewed market interest in works by Renoir. In November 2025, a previously unseen 1890s Renoir depicting the artist’s son and his nanny, Gabrielle Renard, sold for $2 million at Drouot in Paris after being out of public view for a century. This May, Bonhams auctioned 21 additional paintings from Renard’s personal collection , many never before exhibited. Renoir’s auction record remains $78.1 million, set by Dance at Le moulin de la Galette at Sotheby’s New York in 1990. The exhibition arrives in a city with a complicated history with the artist, however. In 2015, protesters calling themselves Renoir Sucks at Painting picketed outside the MFA Boston, arguing the museum should remove his work from view.. This exhibition hopes to reframe the Impressionist’s work for a new generation, focusing on Renoir’s unique emotional connection to themes of modern love and friendship.

title: 5 Art Habits That Can Help You Live Longer
summary: We all know the classic doctor-recommended tenets of healthy living—from getting our daily 10,000 steps to eating our “five a day.” Maintaining these habits can help us live longer, healthier, and happier lives. But recent research has uncovered a new regimen that may help keep our bodies healthier as we age: engaging in the arts. A University College London (UCL) study into epigenetic aging—the biological deterioration of our cells caused by changes in how our DNA is regulated over time—found that creative and cultural activities may affect aging in a way comparable to physical exercise. The study defined arts engagement broadly, from singing, dancing, and painting, to visiting exhibitions, museums, and heritage sites. Observing #71, 2023 Matt Lambert (b. 1982) Gallery Different The findings add to growing interest in art as a health-promoting behavior. Some countries, including the Netherlands and Greece, have even prescribed art for conditions such as depression and cardiovascular disease. But UCL’s study is the first of its kind to show such a connection between the arts and biological age. “There is a growing body of work demonstrating that arts engagement is a health-promoting behavior,” said Daisy Fancourt, the lead author of the study and the head of the Social Biobehavioural Research Group at UCL. “ We should promote creative engagement just like we promote 10,000 steps a day or five-a-day of fruits and vegetables.” The research is part of a £3.5 million ($4.7 million), seven-year program led by UCL and funded by the Wellcome. As that work continues, Fancourt offers five practical ways to make art part of a healthy-aging regimen. Make creativity a regular habit Sleepless creativity, 2021 Aldona Jablonska Klimczak Art Nou Millenni Gallery The UCL research has shown that, overall, the more often people engage in the arts, the lower their biological age may be. In one test, epigenetic aging was 0.8 years lower in people who engaged with the arts weekly and 1.02 years lower among those who did so monthly, compared to those engaging once or twice a year. “Regular, sustained engagement is key,” said Fancourt. She recommends approaching creativity “little and often” so that it becomes part of everyday life. That might mean spending a few minutes drawing or painting, doing 10 minutes of crafting, taking photographs during a walk, or listening closely to a concert. The activity does not need to be ambitious or time-consuming to count. 2. Start small with achievable goals Look, 2015 Rebecca Doughty The Schoolhouse Gallery Fancourt warns against “bingeing on art.” “Just as with crash food diets, you should avoid making major changes to your art ‘intake’ straight away,” she said. “Don’t feel you need to start dozens of new artistic hobbies or sign up to daily art classes, as big behavioural adjustments rarely last. “ Instead, set small, achievable goals for creative tasks that fit naturally into your daily routine. It can also help to schedule artistic activities for times when you tend to feel stressed, sad, tired, or lonely. Like exercise, engaging with art can lift both mood and energy levels, Fancourt says. “In the same way that we structure our food intake to recharge our batteries, you can use art, music, reading, and culture to help regulate your energy or mood,” she told Artsy. 3. Mix up your art diet June Picnic, 2024 Claire Cushman Artemis Gallery McAmerica, 2025 Nicole Santiago First Street Gallery How often you engage with art matters, but variety may be important too. Fancourt’s study found an association between younger biological age and participating in a diverse range of cultural and creative activities. Much as we are encouraged to eat a variety of fruits and vegetables, we may gain more from the arts when we vary what we consume and create . “Each type of arts activity has different effects on us cognitively, emotionally, and physiologically,” Fancourt said. “You should mix up your watching, making, listening, and creating.” Try combining active and receptive experiences. You could visit a gallery one week, attend a concert the next, then spend an afternoon painting, photographing, or making something by hand. 4. Turn online discovery into real-world engagement White dog side view working at window with office plant, 2026 Scott Reeder Saenger Galería Digital platforms have made it easier than ever to discover artists, explore exhibitions, and encounter art from around the world. But Fancourt suggests that, where possible, online engagement should be a starting point rather than the whole experience. “Viewing art on our phones or laptops or participating virtually in activities can dilute some of the health benefits of the arts,” she said. Use digital tools to find artists, galleries, fairs, and exhibitions that interest you, then look for opportunities to experience art in person—whether by visiting a local show, attending a live event, or spending time with a work you own. “Make your daily arts engagement real, not virtual, for maximum effects,” Fancourt said. 5. Give art your full attention At the Museum I, 2020 Toni Hamel Oeno Gallery Mindfulness—the practice of maintaining awareness of our thoughts, feelings, bodily sensations, and surroundings—can be difficult amid the demands of everyday life. But Fancourt says being fully present is an important part of getting the most from an artistic activity. “Take time to savor the experience,” she said. “Whatever creative activity you’re doing, spend some of the time trying to think of nothing other than the art and being entirely present. Resist the urge to multitask.” Put your phone away while visiting an exhibition. Listen to a piece of music without checking your email. When painting, crafting, or reading, focus on the colors, textures, sounds, and emotions of the experience rather than trying to complete another task at the same time. The aim is not simply to fit more art into your day, but to pay attention to it when you do. …It’s never too late to begin Barnett Newman: Vir Heroicus Sublimis/MoMA (Man, Heroic and Sublime), 2023 Joe Fig Cristin Tierney According to the UCL study, the “associations between leisure and epigenetic ageing became more prominent in adults from mid-life.” This means that “the relationship between arts engagement and biological aging becomes larger and more important as we get older,” Fancourt says. So it’s never too late to improve your health through the arts. By making art engagement regular, manageable, varied, physical, and mindful, you may be adding more than enjoyment to your life—you may also be supporting healthier aging.

title: This Dubai Collector Is Amassing an Impressive Collection of Rising South Asian Artists
summary: Kamila Rangoonwala Ahmed grew up around art, but her collection has become distinctly her own. Based in Dubai with deep ties to London and the South Asian subcontinent, she has spent the last decade building a collection rooted in patronage, personal instinct, and a belief in artists at pivotal moments in their careers. Ahmed’s collection moves fluidly between generations of South Asian art. Works by established figures such as Zarina sit alongside those of younger practitioners such as Aiza Ahmed . In its totality, the collection is rooted in history and animated by discovery. How Ahmed’s collection is shaped by her upbringing and instinct Ahmed grew up in a family where collecting was inseparable from cultural support. Her family spent decades supporting and collecting South Asian modern and contemporary art. “My grandfather was a passionate advocate of the arts and believed deeply in the role culture plays in shaping society,” she said. “That appreciation was woven into our family life, so art was never something that felt separate from everyday conversation.” That legacy gave Ahmed an early education in collecting, but her own approach developed through a different lens. Rather than beginning with established names, Ahmed was drawn to artists at the start of their careers. Her collecting journey began in Pakistan at Karachi’s VM Art Gallery “Emerging Talent” exhibition, where graduating students from the country’s leading art schools presented their work to the public. “What drew me was the opportunity to acquire works at such an early stage in an artist’s career and then follow their evolution over time,” she said. “There is something incredibly rewarding about discovering an artist early on and watching their practice develop over the years.” Her draw to emerging artists has become a defining feature of her art buying but is accompanied by works by established South Asian names. These include Francis Newton Souza , Ali Kazim , and Rashid Rana . Building a collection rooted in language, memory, and personal history Ahmed’s eye continues to evolve. What has remained consistent is her attraction to works that engage with language and personal histories. Increasingly, she finds herself drawn to artists who incorporate text into their practice. “Writing carries an emotional weight that transcends language,” she said. “Whether you can read it or not, the rhythm, movement, and presence of text can evoke memory, intimacy and emotion.” Among the works she returns to most often is Sea, Sermon, Story (2022) , a deep blue triptych by Karachi-based artist Anushka Rustomji that explores the sea and sky as ancient, shifting sites for the sacred. “I’ve always been drawn to Anushka’s ability to weave together personal narratives, history, and memory through an incredibly delicate visual language,” Ahmed said. “It’s one of those works that reveals something new every time I spend time with it.” She also speaks similarly about Pakistani artist Bushra Waqas Khan , whose work Sub Rosa (2021) occupies a prominent place in her home. The sculpture’s midsection billows outward, even as the whole form holds itself upright, steady as a mannequin. “I love the way her work combines beauty, craftsmanship, and social commentary while remaining incredibly elegant and visually captivating,” she said. Khan was shortlisted for the 2021 Jameel Art Prize, organized by the Victoria and Albert Museum in partnership with the Dubai institution Art Jameel. Investing in artists before the spotlight Brightly colored works by the neo-miniaturist artist Wardha Shabbir hold a similar significance, particularly given Ahmed’s long relationship with the artist’s practice. Acquired years before Shabbir’s inclusion in the 2026 Venice Biennale main exhibition, “ In Minor Keys ,” they reflect a recurring pattern within the collection of identifying artists at the early stages of their careers. “Having followed her career for many years now, it is incredibly rewarding to watch her practice evolve,” she said. “My advice is always to buy what genuinely resonates with you rather than what you think you should buy.” Her latest acquisition continues that trajectory. She is currently acquiring a work by New York–based artist Aiza Ahmed , whose practice has recently explored the Attari-Wagah border ceremony, enacted daily by the military on the border of India and Pakistan since 1959. “As someone whose own life has been shaped by connections across Karachi, Dubai and London, I found the work deeply resonant,” she said. Still, like many collectors, Ahmed can recall a few works that got away . She points to a bench by Rana Begum at Art Dubai in the early 2010s. “At the time, it felt like a significant purchase, and I hesitated,” she said. “Looking back, not only has the value increased substantially, but it was also such a beautiful example of her practice.” More recently, she missed a work by Misha Japanwala , whose sculptural practice explores the body and questions around self-representation. “I would have loved to have added one of her moulded works to my collection,” Ahmed said. Ahmed’s collection captures a generation of South Asian artists at a moment of extraordinary international visibility. But its real strength lies in the quieter years before that visibility arrived. Her collection is not only a record of where South Asian art is now, but of the artists she chose to believe in before the wider world caught up.

title: The Whitney to stage major Roy Lichtenstein exhibition in October 2026.
summary: This fall, the Whitney Museum of American Art will open “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New,” a survey of more than 130 works tracing the artist’s career from the early 1940s through the 1990s, opening on October 11th. Organized by curator Meg Onli with artist Alex Da Corte as guest curator, the exhibition moves beyond Lichtenstein ’s Pop -era surfaces to focus on his preoccupation with how images are copied, enlarged, circulated, and altered as they travel. Spanning painting, drawing, collage, prints, sculpture, and film, the show promises a fresh look at one of the 20th century’s defining names. Notably, the exhibition will reunite all eight works from Lichtenstein’s 1962 debut at Leo Castelli Gallery for the first time. The exhibition also includes recreations of three murals, among them a nearly 96-foot-long iteration of Greene Street Mural (1983), and an outdoor presentation of Girl in Window (1964) realized by Da Corte. The checklist draws on Lichtenstein’s best-known paintings, including Look Mickey (1961), Drowning Girl (1963), Happy Tears (1964), and Artist’s Studio ‘The Dance’ (1974). The Whitney show also features artists who absorbed Lichtenstein’s ideas about copying and authorship, including Louise Lawler , Richard Pettibone , and Sturtevant . The exhibition frames Lichtenstein’s images as newly relevant in an age of digital cropping, filtering, and reposting. It will argue that the artist understood that pictures are unstable well before digital circulation made that condition universal. “ Like New ” arrives amid a broader wave of institutional attention to Lichtenstein. The Dallas Museum of Art and the Nasher Sculpture Center are jointly presenting “ Roy Lichtenstein in the Studio ” through mid-August, while the Guggenheim Museum ’s “Guggenheim Pop” remains on view through January 2027. Timed tickets for “Like New” are on sale now; member previews run October 8th through 10th ahead of the public opening.

title: Fashion retailer Pull & Bear launches photography prize.
summary: Pull & Bear, the youth fashion retailer, is launching its own international photography prize as part of the Festival of Fashion, Photography and Accessories–Hyères. Founded in 1986, the French competition has helped launch the careers of designers including Viktor & Rolf , Anthony Vaccarello, and Julien Dossena. The “Prix de la Photographie de Mode Pull & Bear” will debut as a new category within the festival’s official photography competition at the 41st edition of Festival de Hyères, running October 15th through 18th at Villa Noailles in southeast France, the modernist estate designed by Robert Mallet-Stevens. The winner, announced October 17th, will receive €20,000 ($22,816), making it an equal purse to the festival’s existing “Grand Prix du Jury Photographie 7L,” backed by the Chanel-owned publishing house 7L, which was founded by Karl Lagerfeld . Beyond the cash prize, the winner will produce a campaign or commissioned photographic project for Pull & Bear, see their work promoted across the brand’s platforms and flagship stores, and collaborate on a capsule T-shirt collection under the label’s “Pull&Bear × The Photographer Project.” A fanzine and a solo exhibition at Villa Noailles during the 2027 festival will follow. The launch arrives as fashion photography competes for attention with short-form video on platforms like TikTok. Founded in 1986 as a platform for emerging designers, Festival de Hyères added its photography competition in 1997 and a separate accessories prize in 2016, becoming an important platform for discovering new generations of creators. The brand said in an interview that the new award was created “to discover and support a new generation of artists who transcend the traditional codes of fashion photography.” Ten finalists from countries including China, Switzerland, Japan, Italy, and France—among them Xue Ling Chen, Zacharie Lewertoff, and Valeria Sarto —will compete for the inaugural Pull & Bear prize alongside the festival’s other photography honors. The jury is led by French photographer Camille Vivier, with members including Sylvie Lécallier, head of the photography collection at the Palais Galliera, and Noémie Ninot, winner of last year’s Grand Prix du Jury Photographie 7L. Pull & Bear joins a roster of sponsors—including 7L and the French label American Vintage, which funds its own €15,000 ($17,115) photography award at the festival—as the Inditex-owned brand expands its presence in cultural patronage. The move positions the retailer alongside institutions with longer histories in fashion photography, betting that a direct stake in one of the industry’s established talent pipelines will translate into visibility for both emerging photographers and the brand itself.

title: 5 Stunning Art Exhibitions to See on the Mediterranean in Summer 2026
summary: There is an ancient saying that the Mediterranean extends as far as the olive tree grows. While the ocean itself spans Europe, Asia, and Africa, there is a shared culture that binds its countries well beyond its coastlines and shrubland; it includes a particular relationship with beauty and slowness. Nowhere is this sentiment more pronounced than when it comes to art. In most cases, taking in a great exhibition sits easily in the same itinerary as a swim and a long lunch. So follow the olive trees and the scent of salt and dry earth. For a last-minute summer escape, the Mediterranean is hard to beat. And this summer, if you love art, you’re in luck. From Marseille, France, to the Greek islands, some of the most compelling shows of the year are taking place in Mediterranean destinations. Taken together, this group of shows suggests that art, like most things along the Med, is something to be experienced with your senses and can fit seamlessly into a perfect day. Here, we share five shows taking place in Mediterranean destinations that are worth booking a trip for. Barcelona “Gaudí-Miró-Gomis: Deconstructed” Casa Batlló Through Jan. 10, 2027 There is no separating Antoni Gaudí from Barcelona. Most visitors come to the city exactly to see his designs: the eclectic, phantasmagoric architecture which can be enjoyed along with the beaches and fever of a city that places fun and leisure at the forefront. This summer, the Gaudí–designed Casa Batlló is making the case that the artist’s world was far from isolated. “Gaudí-Miró-Gomis: Deconstructed,” which runs until January 10, 2027, brings Joan Miró ’s sculptures and graphic works into the eclectic, undulating interiors of the house Gaudí built between 1904 and 1906, alongside Joaquim Gomis’s photographs of Miró and his Barcelona circle. These artists occupied the same city at different times, yet shared several of each other’s sensibilities. The seed of the show is a single photograph by Gomis: Miró and his circle, on the terrace of Casa Batlló itself. From that image, curators have reconstructed a whole web of influence. The London-based art and design studio Tomorrow Bureau adds a contemporary layer, with 3D scans, animation, and generative video, that makes visitors look at Miró’s forms as if for the first time, finding Gaudí’s organic geometries hiding inside them.Once in Barcelona, don’t miss the Fundació Joan Miró on the hill above the city: the artist’s meditative world is the perfect counterpoint to Barcelona’s lively movida scene. Marseille Adrien Vescovi “Dormir comme le soleil” Vieille Charité Through Jan. 10, 2027 Known for its sea, sun, and mistral, Marseille is often referred to as the Berlin of the Mediterranean. Marseille’s culture is built on the coast, its identity both layered and harmoniously contradictory. Strong Arab and African presences shape its neighborhoods and its food; a queer scene rooted in places like La Plaine gives it its edge. Waves of Parisians and expats who arrived after the pandemic have added a certain polish without quite taming it. It is the natural home for the “Saison Méditerranée,” a sprawling series of art events running through January 2027; its anchor show is Adrien Vescovi ’s “Dormir comme le soleil” at the Vieille Charité museum. Vescovi has draped the 17th-century stone arcades of the building with monumental dyed textiles, built from old bedsheets and natural pigments. This poetic and delicate operation is reminiscent of Christo and Jeanne-Claude —using textiles to modify our perception of architecture—and of the colored windows of la Cité Radieuse , Le Corbusier ’s building in Marseille. Once you’re in the city, also check out French artist Louisa Babari's “AFRICA” at the MAC, a show exploring the mythologies of North Africa through photographic, visual, and sound art. The MUCEM—dedicated to Mediterranean cultures—is worth visiting. Chios, Greece “Letter to an Ailing Father” DEO Projects Through Aug. 30 When thinking about Greek islands, most think of Mykonos and Santorini. But art lovers should also consider Chios, less than an hour’s flight from Athens, and known for its black-and-white mastic villages and the tranquil beaches of the pristine Aegean Sea. DEO Projects, the only contemporary art organization on Chios, has staged “Letter to an Ailing Father” inside the classrooms and corridors of a centuries-old school in the mountains above the village of Volissos, where the medieval stone architecture has barely changed in centuries. This is perhaps the last place you would expect to find work by international stars such as Cindy Sherman and Danh Võ , alongside selections from beloved Mediterranean artists such as Evi Kalogiropoulou and Eleni Odysseos . Some 14 artists from 11 countries have responded to the figure of the father as authority, as absence, as diminishment. The exhibition includes painting, textiles, sound, video, and new commissions alongside existing works, curated by Akis Kokkinos, a famed Mediterranean curator. Naples Maria Lai “Essere è tessere ” Madre Museum Through Sep. 21 Sip a quick espresso at a shop counter—that’s how Neapolitans do it—and throw yourself into the narrow streets of Spaccanapoli. The artery divides the city in two and is blessed by a divine afternoon light reminiscent of the images of saints populating the many beautiful churches that line your path. Deeply pagan yet profoundly Christian, Naples is a city where soccer icons live on the street beside images of the Madonna, where the people hustle and bustle and make the city magical and alive like nowhere else. It is excessive, gorgeous, and unapologetically itself. Inside this creative chaos, the Madre Museum is an oasis of sorts. White and pristine within, its windows frame the city outside: buildings half-crumbled, beautiful and decadent, a view of Mount Vesuvius on the horizon. In a city that feels like a web, Maria Lai ’s solo exhibition “Essere è tessere” (which translates to “being is weaving”) is particularly fitting. The sweeping retrospective gathers 200 works across six decades of the late artist’s career: sewn books, woven canvases, the threads and fables that made Lai one of postwar Italy’s strangest and most tender visionaries. Malta Reggie Burrows Hodges “Mela” MICAS Through Aug. 30 Culturally, Malta is tufo-white and ottanio in its colors. The island is a place of unique pairings; namely, contrasting elements that surprisingly complement each other. Walk the streets of its capital city Valletta, and you’ll catch flashes of London in the colors of the window frames and the ironwork on the balconies, then something closer to Jeddah in the mashrabiya-style screens that shade the facades, then turn a corner and think, for a moment, that you’re in Sicily. That’s what makes Malta captivating . A place not to miss: MICAS, a museum built into a 17th-century fortification. Its new steel-and- glass roof rises inside the bastions of Floriana while the limestone ramparts look out over Marsamxett Harbor. What’s inside this summer earns the journey twice over: “Mela,” American artist Reggie Burrows Hodges’s first European solo show. The survey fills all four gallery floors with 30 new paintings made after the artist relocated his studio to Malta for two years, absorbing the island’s coastline, its construction workers, and its quality of light. The centerpiece is a monumental canvas painted in direct response to Caravaggio’s Beheading of Saint John the Baptist (1608), which hangs across the harbor in St. John’s Co-Cathedral, and is a must-see once there.

title: Pakistani artist Misha Japanwala’s designs feature in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey.”
summary: Pakistani artist and fashion designer Misha Japanwala created two sculptural pieces worn by Lupita Nyong’o in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , marking a prominent film placement for the artist best known for body-cast sculpture. Nyong’o, who plays both Helen of Troy and her vengeful half-sister Clytemnestra in Nolan’s epic, recommended Japanwala to costume designer Ellen Mirojnick while the pair discussed how to dress the Queen of Sparta (the artist had previous produced a custom breastplate for Nyong’o, which she wore to the 2023 Tony Awards). Japanwala's body castings in bronze and resin often explore scarring, asymmetry, and the human form. In the first work she made for the film, she produced a bronze, asymmetrical neck and shoulder plate for Nyong’o's character. “To me, it looked like a broken statue,” Mirojnick said of the work in an interview with W magazine , describing how she built the piece into a capelet worn atop a ruched, draped gown. Japanwala told Artsy that for this work she "layered copper and brass metallic coatings to add depth, and then added a brown patina on the surface.” Another of Japanwala’s works appears in Helen’s final scene, as she bids farewell to Telemachus (Tom Holland). Here, a gold choker by Japanwala is paired with a chainmail-like caftan-gown that Mirojnick sourced in Spain. “I am so proud of how both of the works turned out and the way they are illuminated in the film,” Japanwala added. “As an artist, it means a lot that Ellen Mirojnick and Sara O’ Donnell, the amazing costume designers, were willing to put in the time and effort to work with an independent artist like me to bring these pieces to life.” Japanwala, who trained at Parsons School of Design and worked at Elle and the womenswear and accessories brand Proenza Schouler before turning to sculpture full time. She has built a practice around casting bodies—breasts, torsos, stretch marks, scars—as a rejection of conventional beauty standards. In an interview with Artsy , Japanwala said she hopes her works help people to “meet [their] body where it’s at, to be grateful for it and to understand and appreciate it and allow it to carry [them] through life.” Represented by Hannah Traore in New York, she staged her first solo show, “ Beghairati Ki Nishaani–Traces of Shamelessness ” in 2023, followed by “Topographies” at the EXPO Chicago art fair in 2024 and “ Sarsabzi ” at Traore’s gallery last fall. Her work has also included a viral body cast of Cardi B for the singer’s pregnancy announcement, and she has been profiled in both Indian and American Vogue . Japanwala’s contribution to The Odyssey is a major moment of recognition for the artist, bringing her interest in the body to one of the major cinematic moments of the year. “This past week has felt surreal and like a dream!” Japanwala added.“I got to see the film on opening day, and I teared up when Lupita first appeared on screen as Helen of Troy wearing one of the sculptures. Her performance is breathtaking and I am just over the moon that I get to be a tiny part of bringing that character to life.”

title: 5 Epic Artworks to Explore after Seeing Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey”
summary: Greek Myths, 2021 Chris Ofili Victoria Miro Prologue to Troy, 1974 Romare Bearden RoGallery Originating around 3,000 years ago, The Odyssey remains one of the most influential works of literature ever. This ancient Greek epic poem recounts the story of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, and his perilous 10-year journey home following the Trojan War, encountering man-eating monsters, vengeful gods, and countless temptations. Despite its fantastical nature, the poem has an enduring appeal today, with a highly anticipated film adaptation from Christopher Nolan bringing Homer’s epic back into public conversation. After all, the epic explores universal human concerns such as displacement, identity, fate, free will, resilience, and the search for home. These themes have made The Odyssey a continual source of inspiration for artists across centuries, as it remains a powerful metaphor for the human search for meaning, purpose, and home. Here are five contemporary artworks that engage with Homer’s enduring epic. Romare Bearden “A Black Odyssey ,” 1977 Home to Ithaca, from the Odysseus Series, 1979 Romare Bearden Heritage Auctions “A Black Odyssey” is one of Romare Bearden ’s most ambitious and comprehensive bodies of work. Created in 1977, the series consists of 20 collages inspired by Homer’s epic tale, demonstrating Bearden’s lifelong interest in journeys, migration, and the search for home. Here, Bearden stretched the concept of collage by connecting different histories and experiences, creating what he described as a “global cultural collage.” By reimagining the myth with a cast of entirely Black figures in Benin, with Odysseus as an African hero, Bearden illuminates the connection between the ancient longing for home and the modern African American experience, drawing on his own experience of the Great Migration and the wider legacy of the transatlantic slave trade. Speaking of his series, the artist explained : “It is universal. So if a child in Benin or in Louisiana…sees my paintings of Odysseus, he can understand the myth better.” Though he remains faithful to the spirit of the story, Bearden takes certain artistic liberties in his interpretation. In Home to Ithaca (1977), geometric buildings line a harbor (presumably Ithaca, Odysseus’s long-sought destination) as a sailboat approaches. In The Odyssey , Homer relays that Odysseus was asleep on his ship’s deck when his vessel sailed into Ithaca’s harbor, whereas Bearden instead depicts him standing proudly atop the ship’s bow, highlighting the endurance and determination that has carried him through his long journey. Rather than presenting the voyage as a heroic conquest, as in the original epic, Bearden’s interpretation focuses on the resilience of the human spirit through adversity, reflecting his belief that “Life is going to triumph somehow.” Paul Chan La Baigneur 7 (Teenyelemachus), 2018 Contemporary multimedia artist Paul Chan was struck by the Greek word polytropos which appears in The Odyssey ’s opening line. It’s used to describe Odysseus, and translates as “infinitely cunning” adaptable, or resourceful. In his essay “Odysseus as Artist” (2017), Chan argues that these qualities are essential not only to Odysseus but also to the role of the artist in contemporary society. This idea became the foundation for Chan’s 2018 exhibition “Odysseus and the Bathers” at the Museum of Cycladic Art, Athens, where he explored how creativity can find new paths when traditional methods become limiting. Inspired by Odysseus’s ability to “cheat his own fate,” Chan developed kinetic nylon sculptures. In one, an inflatable, human-like figure stands bent forward at the waist, weighed down by a brightly colored towel hanging from its clasped arms. Electrical cords plugged into casual shoes snake across the floor in various directions, creating a disparate but connected network. As air fills the figure, it jerks and strains until it finally becomes fully upright; then, the ridges on its back disturb the airflow, causing the figure to collapse. Animated by air from specifically modified industrial fans, the artist governs the figures’ movements by directing airflow to the internal structure of the bodies, reflecting how individuals are at the mercy of external forces. The work’s title, La Baigneur 7 (Teenyelemachus) (2018) , playfully alludes to Telemachus, the son of Odysseus and Penelope, a play on words referencing his neons’ glitchy movements. This repeated cycle of the figure continuously attempting—and failing—to remain standing represents Telemachus’s rising up in the face of challenges owing to the absence of his father. Chris Ofili Kiss (Odysseus & Calypso), 2019 Chris Ofili was inspired by The Odyssey after hearing the opening of Emily Wilson’s 2017 translation read aloud by his friend, the curator Okwui Enwezor , in 2018. The phrase “a complicated man” struck a chord, leading him to see Odysseus as a restless and adventurous figure. Its vivid descriptions inspired Ofili to create a series of paintings and drawings based on the poem for his “ Dangerous Liaisons ” exhibition at David Zwirner in 2019. Ofili’s series reinterprets the ancient epic through a contemporary and Caribbean lens: Calypso, for instance, is reimagined as a mermaid, influenced in part by the music of Trinidad, where he has lived since 2005. In Kiss (Odysseus & Calypso) (2019), the pair are shown in a sensual underwater embrace. Odysseus is depicted with dark skin and coiled hair, while Calypso appears as a luminous figure, a nod to Homer’s descriptions of “lustrous Calypso” and the “nymph with lovely braids.” Layered with watercolor, charcoal, oil pastel, graphite, and the artist’s signature gold leaf, the work shimmers with kaleidoscopic richness. The vibrant colors and swirling arabesque forms envelop the figures, creating a lush, otherworldly realm that evokes the allure of the myth. Ellen Gallagher Ecstatic Draught of Fishes , 2020 Ellen Gallagher became particularly interested in The Odyssey in the 1990s. She was drawn to the concept of nostos —the Greek word for “homecoming” or “return”—which first appears in the epic and gave rise to the English word nostalgia. The complexity of the idea resonated with the artist; it is not simply about returning home, but also about the journey. This idea resonates with Gallagher’s own practice, inspired by the Afrofuturist myth of Drexciya—an imagined underwater civilization descended from enslaved Africans thrown overboard during the transatlantic slave trade. Gallagher’s multilayered mixed-media painting Ecstatic Draught of Fishes (2020) (also the title of a 2021 exhibition at Hauser & Wirth ) connects to The Odyssey through its exploration of displacement and the search for home. Gallagher creates a submerged world populated by silver-gray figures, reminiscent of sculptures by the Central African Fang culture. In small clusters, the figures drift along braided, root-like strands that weave horizontally across the composition against a shimmering, mottled surface made up of layers of collaged penmanship paper, paint, and metallic palladium leaf. By reimagining the Atlantic Ocean, Gallagher transforms the epic journey of The Odyssey into a Black Atlantic narrative. Exploring what it means to navigate identity, memory, and belonging across time and space, she offers an alternative mythology encompassing both survival and homecoming. SUPERFLEX Super Kello , 2026 Named after the Finnish word for bell, Super Kello (2026) is a bell-shaped stone sculpture by the Copenhagen-based group SUPERFLEX . Located in the harbor of Kello in Haukipudas, Finland, the pink marble structure faces out to sea like a lighthouse, forging a connection between the human community on land and the marine life below the water. Denmark is one of the flattest countries in the world, and SUPERFLEX’s work acknowledges the rising sea levels of a rapidly changing climate. Indeed, in an interview the group noted that any permanent public art commission may no longer be designed for humans, but for fish. With this in mind, the sculpture is made from modular building blocks known as “fish cubes” developed in collaboration with KWY studio, which maximize the surface area of a cube, creating habitable spaces for marine life. The artwork also invites viewers to reflect on different experiences of time. The work will broadcast Pentti Saarikoski’s Finnish translation of The Odyssey , read by local fisherwoman Elina Halonen, who will read one word per hour over the course of 10 years. By stretching the duration of the artwork over a decade, it invites visitors to slow down and experience time differently while referencing long-term, difficult-to-comprehend processes such as climate change. Just as Odysseus spent years journeying across the sea, the drawn-out, meditative narration also mirrors the duration of Odysseus’s 10-year voyage home. Browse more artworks that channel the epic poem in “Visions of the Odyssey”

title: The Armory Show announces around 230 exhibitors for its 2026 edition.
summary: The Armory Show has revealed the first details of its 2026 edition. The fair will return to New York’s Javits Center from September 24th to 27th, bringing together around 230 galleries from more than 30 countries. This year’s edition will place an emphasis on artists and galleries from the Caribbean and its diasporas through two curator-led sections. Meanwhile, the fair’s Solo and Presents sections have also grown by more than 20 percent. “The Armory Show has always reflected New York’s openness: to artists, galleries and ideas from across the Americas and the wider world,” Kyla McMillan, director of the fair, said in a statement. “This year, that comes through in the breadth of the gallery list, the expansion of Presents and Solo, and the work of our curators, whose sections trace histories of movement, exchange and cultural connection through the Caribbean.” This year’s curated sections take the Caribbean Sea and its surrounding regions as their point of departure. The Platform section, organized this year by SculptureCenter curator Jovanna Venegas, will feature large-scale installations exploring themes of resilience, reconstruction, and technological forms from across the Caribbean. Notable artist projects in the section will include Bony Ramirez , Curtis Talwst Santiago , Lucia Hierro , Rafael Domenech , María Magdalena Campos-Pons , Hew Locke , and Margarita Cabrera . Meanwhile, Focus, curated by María Elena Ortiz of the Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth , will spotlight artists working across the Caribbean and its diasporas through solo and dual-artist presentations featuring, among others, Gio Swaby , Kachelle Knowles , Renée Cox , and Lizania Cruz . The fair’s expanded Solo section will include around 25 single-artist presentations, including Ayako Rokkaku , Betsabeé Romero , José Bechara , and Henry Glavin . The Presents section, devoted to younger galleries, will feature approximately 55 exhibitors, including first-time participants such as Circle Art Gallery , Galerie Noah Klink , Rajiv Menon Contemporary , and Yiwei Gallery , alongside returning exhibitors including Hannah Traore , Hesse Flatow, The Pit, and Reservoir. El Museo del Barrio has also been selected as the recipient of this year's Armory Spotlight, an initiative that provides a complimentary booth to a New York cultural institution. The museum will present work by the textile artist Lulu Varona , who will invite visitors to participate in the creation of one of her works during the fair.

title: How Artwork Pricing Works—and How to Know if You’re Getting a Good Deal
summary: $ (4), 1982 Andy Warhol Avant Gallery The art market is notoriously opaque, especially when it comes to pricing. Unlike most luxury goods, art does not have fixed pricing formulas or regulatory bodies that determine value.
